items.title: Victor Rendon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, November 15, 2019 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Fernando Ortiz, I don’t know if you know that name, he was a Cuban anthropologist who was actually the first to bring out the batá drumming meaning to the public

ctx.x: Okay. Good answer. Your band mates speak of this music with great reverence for its history and lineage and yesterday’s lecture-demonstration was a lot about spirituality. But the music exists in the spiritual realm as well as the secular realm. It is — what might happen — I’ll rephrase. Would there be something that a person could do with this music that would be irreverent and frowned upon? If you’re playing music that’s connected with spirituality and deities, can it be abused?

It can be. We’ve come a long way on that. Back in the — I’ll go back to the early 1900s, Fernando Ortiz, I don’t know if you know that name, he was a Cuban anthropologist who was actually the first to bring out the batá drumming meaning to the public, because back then it was sort of like secretive, Cascadú spoke about you could be actually punished for playing those drums in public. But it was also in respect to the deities. And even it went on also up to the 80s, when I first came to New York in 1980 I tried to…

something to it, I’m not even sure I should say, there’s something inside the drum that it called ayan. So you’re not supposed to bring those drums out into the open. So if somebody did that, yes, that would be an abuse of that culture, of maybe even the deities you know. So you don’t want to do that. Also those drums, when they’re used in a religious ceremony they’re supposed to be put away at least before dark. So you play from 12 to 6 or whenever and then you put them away. They’re never supposed to touch the…
